task:
Questions:

### absorb16.Q1
A project keeps two curated collections, each governed by its own charter: a set of requirements, and a set of acceptance checks whose charter says the checks exist to verify the requirements. Each check names the requirements it verifies. You are asked whether the set of checks is complete. What do you measure it against, and how do you treat (i) a requirement that no check names, (ii) a check that names no requirement, and (iii) a check that names three requirements?

### absorb16.Q2
In a body of guidance organised into sets, each with a charter, can a relation between two sets be anything other than a boundary - one set telling itself apart from a neighbour? If it can, give an example of the kind, and say where such a relation should be recorded.

### absorb16.Q3
You are the judge at a gate that passes only if a data migration on a production database succeeded. You have no access to that database. The agent that ran the migration gives you its own log, which ends 'migration complete, 0 errors'. Can you pass the gate on that log? What, if anything, would let you pass it?

### absorb16.Q4
A member of a curated set is upgraded from a placeholder version to a full one, without changing what it is for. Does it keep its identifier? If the set's members come in such tiers, where should that be stated?

### absorb16.Q5
A test suite passed against a simulator that faithfully models the network but has no model of disk failure. A colleague writes 'the system survives faults'. What may the result support, and how should it be stated?

### absorb16.Q6
A member that has been in use for months is rewritten as a better version. While it was in use, three defects in it were found and recorded. What happens to that record when it is rewritten, and to any earlier statement about the member that turns out to be wrong?

### absorb16.Q7
Two sets: one of procedures, and one of kinds of work, where each kind of work names the procedures that conduct it. Someone proposes keeping, in the procedures set's charter, a hand-maintained table of which kinds of work cite each procedure. What is wrong with that, and how should that view be kept?

### absorb16.Q8
You are investigating whether a set is complete. You propose a way to cut its population into cells, by the situations its members address. One member fits none of the cells, and another fits every cell. What does that tell you, and what do you do?

Write your answers to this file, and nothing else:
  {WORKSPACE}/answers.md
Put each answer under its heading exactly as given above (a line starting with ###), and use no other headings inside an answer. End with a final heading `### OBSERVATIONS` noting anything ambiguous, inconsistent or wrong you met, or "none".
When the file is written, reply with only the word DONE.

properties.key: Measure the checks against the requirements' population: the checks set's scope is another set's members, so each requirement is a cell, and which checks verify which requirement is read from the checks' own declarations, not from a table kept by hand. (i) is a gap in the checks set, the set whose purpose includes the relation, and goes to the backlog naming that set. (ii) is a finding: the check is outside the set's scope, or it shows a requirement the requirements set lacks. (iii) is not a defect: a covering member may cover several members, and that does not show the cut is wrong.
properties.rubric: Elements: (a) completeness is measured against the requirements' population, each requirement checked for a covering check; (b) a requirement no check names is a gap in the checks set; (c) a check naming no requirement is a finding - outside the checks set's scope, or a sign the requirements set is missing a member - not simply acceptable; (d) a check naming three requirements is acceptable and is not evidence that the way the population was cut is wrong. 2 for all four. 1 for three of the four. 0 otherwise.
properties.question: A project keeps two curated collections, each governed by its own charter: a set of requirements, and a set of acceptance checks whose charter says the checks exist to verify the requirements. Each check names the requirements it verifies. You are asked whether the set of checks is complete. What do you measure it against, and how do you treat (i) a requirement that no check names, (ii) a check that names no requirement, and (iii) a check that names three requirements?

properties.key: Yes. One set can exist to cover another set's members - for example, every procedure cited by some kind of work, or every check covering some requirement - and that relation is not a boundary. It is declared once, on the members of the side whose meaning includes it, with the reverse view generated from those declarations; the covering set's charter says in its scope that it covers the other set, but which members are covered is never kept in the charter.
properties.rubric: Elements: (a) yes, with an example in which members of one set cover, verify, cite or are required by members of another; (b) the relation is recorded once, as declarations on the members of one side, with any reverse view derived from them rather than kept by hand on both sides or written into a charter. 2 for both. 1 for (a) alone. 0 for (b) alone or otherwise, including answering that every relation between sets is a boundary.
properties.question: In a body of guidance organised into sets, each with a charter, can a relation between two sets be anything other than a boundary - one set telling itself apart from a neighbour? If it can, give an example of the kind, and say where such a relation should be recorded.

properties.key: No. The agent's own log settles what the agent reported, not what happened. The gate could pass only if the judge could re-run the work, or check the report against a record the agent could not have written, such as one produced by the database or its platform. With neither, the judge says so - the gate's condition is not shown - rather than passing it.
properties.rubric: Elements: (a) not on that log alone, because it is the acting party's own report of its own conduct; (b) passing needs either re-running or re-checking the work, or a record the agent could not have written; (c) with neither available, the judge reports the condition as not shown or unverified rather than passing it. 2 for all three. 1 for (a) with one of the others. 0 otherwise, including passing the gate on the log.
properties.question: You are the judge at a gate that passes only if a data migration on a production database succeeded. You have no access to that database. The agent that ran the migration gives you its own log, which ends 'migration complete, 0 errors'. Can you pass the gate on that log? What, if anything, would let you pass it?

properties.key: It keeps its identifier: an edit in place keeps the id, and only changing the identifier makes it a replacement, which retires the old one. Tiers are kinds of member, so the set's charter states once what kinds exist and how a member is told which it is; no member states it about its siblings.
properties.rubric: Elements: (a) it keeps its identifier, since changing the identifier would make it a replacement or retirement rather than an edit; (b) the tiers are stated once for the set as a whole - in its charter or governing document, as kinds of member and how a member is told which it is - not separately in each member. 2 for both. 1 for one. 0 for neither.
properties.question: A member of a curated set is upgraded from a placeholder version to a full one, without changing what it is for. Does it keep its identifier? If the set's members come in such tiers, where should that be stated?

properties.key: Only claims about what the simulator models: behaviour under network faults. Behaviour under disk failure is not shown and must be stated as unverified. The claim itself must be narrowed to what was tested and say what the stand-in leaves out, rather than left broad with a caveat attached; a stand-in whose omissions cannot be stated is not a valid proxy.
properties.rubric: Elements: (a) the result supports only the claim about network faults; (b) disk-failure behaviour is stated as not shown or unverified; (c) the claim itself is narrowed, or states what the simulator leaves out, rather than kept broad with a caveat beside it. 2 for all three. 1 for (a) and (b). 0 otherwise.
properties.question: A test suite passed against a simulator that faithfully models the network but has no model of disk failure. A colleague writes 'the system survives faults'. What may the result support, and how should it be stated?

properties.key: The record is kept: what was found stays readable as written, and the rewritten member carries forward what was learned. An earlier statement found wrong is kept under a correction banner, beside what replaced it, rather than silently deleted or rewritten.
properties.rubric: Elements: (a) the record of the three defects is kept, not deleted or overwritten; (b) an earlier statement found wrong is retained and marked as corrected, not silently edited away. 2 for both. 1 for one. 0 for neither.
properties.question: A member that has been in use for months is rewritten as a better version. While it was in use, three defects in it were found and recorded. What happens to that record when it is rewritten, and to any earlier statement about the member that turns out to be wrong?

properties.key: The relation is already declared once, on the side whose meaning includes it - each kind of work names its procedures - so a hand-kept table is a second statement of one fact, free to drift and to omit what nobody remembered to add. The reverse view is generated from the declarations, never maintained by hand.
properties.rubric: Elements: (a) the table restates relations already declared on the kinds of work, so the two can disagree or drift; (b) the view should be generated or derived from those declarations, not maintained by hand. 2 for both. 1 for one. 0 for neither, including endorsing the table.
properties.question: Two sets: one of procedures, and one of kinds of work, where each kind of work names the procedures that conduct it. Someone proposes keeping, in the procedures set's charter, a hand-maintained table of which kinds of work cite each procedure. What is wrong with that, and how should that view be kept?

properties.key: That the cut is probably wrong: a member that fits nowhere, or everywhere, is evidence the partition is wrong. Revise or replace the partition, and state why the new one was chosen, rather than treating the members as defective or forcing them into cells.
properties.rubric: Elements: (a) both observations count as evidence that the way the population was cut is wrong; (b) the partition is revised or replaced, rather than the members rejected or forced to fit. 2 for both. 1 for (a) alone, or for treating only one of the two members as evidence and revising. 0 otherwise, including concluding that the members are defective.
properties.question: You are investigating whether a set is complete. You propose a way to cut its population into cells, by the situations its members address. One member fits none of the cells, and another fits every cell. What does that tell you, and what do you do?

notes: Tests the absorption of pull request 16 (M7.2, rulings 0109-0111): Q1 to Q3 probe the absorbed concepts (coverage between sets, investigating a covering set, a party's own report); Q4 to Q7 probe concepts the triage judged already covered; Q8 guards the partition misfit test the proposal deleted.
